newsitem.title: UK: British financial markets wary of Labour landslide.
newsitem.headline: British financial markets wary of Labour landslide.

text.p: British financial markets may be relaxed about the prospect of the opposition Labour party winning the election, but if the party achieves a landslide victory there could be a short-term sell-off, economists said.

"If there was a landslide for Labour with a 100 to 150 seat majority and the Conservatives were set to be a weak opposition then the markets would react negatively, at least initially," said Deborah Read, economist at Bank America.

The danger, analysts say, is that Labour may feel empowered by a clear victory to revert to more traditional hard-line policies, moving back towards a more left-of-centre policy agenda which the party favoured in the 1980s and 1990s.

Many rank and file members of the party, hungry for leftist policies after almost 18 years of Conservative rule, may quickly become impatient if a clear win does not result in bold policy initiatives, analysts said.

"A Labour parliamentary majority of 100 to 150 seats would leave the markets feeling distinctly uncomfortable and more than 150 would be a significant worry," said Don Smith, economist at HSBC Markets.
Labour currently lead Prime Minister John Major's beleaguered government by around 20 points in the opinion polls, suggesting a landslide victory for Labour is a real possibility.
Labour achieved a massive 17 percent swing in its favour to win the recent by-election in the northern England constituency of Wirral South, traditionally a safe Conservative seat.

A Reuter survey of 20 voting experts published on March 5 found on average they expect Labour to win with an overall parliamentary majority of 59 -- more than enough to lead from the front without coalitions for a full parliamentary term but some way short of a landslide.
But some experts are more bullish on Labour's chances.

"I had expected some signs of a Conservative recovery (in the polls), but the Wirral by-election put paid to that. There is evidence of direct switching of allegiances in Wirral on a large scale," said Peter Kellner, an independent political analyst, who sees Labour winning 93 more seats than all the other parties combined.

Since the Second World War the radicalism and boldness of British governments has been largely governed by the size of their parliamentary majorities, most recently demonstrated by the 1980s governments under Margaret Thatcher which were emboldened by majorities of 144 in 1983 and 101 in 1987.

The current premiership of John Major, by contrast, has been marked by consensual policies, pragmatism and gravitation towards the political centre, reflecting a slim majority of just 21 achieved in the 1992 election.

"The markets have discounted a Labour win and are comfortable with the idea. However, markets do want an effective check on a Labour government -- such as a Conservative opposition party which has some clout and is not overwhelmed in all parliamentary votes," said Read of Bank America.
Read reckons a landslide Labour win could see an initial fall in the sterling exchange rate against major currencies of some two percent, with 10-year gilt yields jumping 20 to 25 basis points.

But, after initial jitters in the week following the election expected on May 1, the markets are likely to calm down as the party enjoys a honeymoon period, particularly if it turns out to be more friendly towards European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) than the Major government.

"The crucial issue if Labour wins a landslide will be whether they decide they have a clear mandate to go out and spend and please their core supporters, or whether it simply encourages them to aim for two-terms in office, where they please the financial markets first and reward their supporters later," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.

"I actually think a landslide win -- which looks a real possibility -- could actually result in the party being tougher rather than more expansionary, establishing its credentials with the markets," Lyons said.
